rows.name: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3625

topics_app: The Office of the Judge (Kitab Al-Aqdiyah)

rows.detail: The Prophet appointed agents: Urwah al-Bariqi to buy a sacrificial animal, agents to collect zakat, Jabir at Khaybar — graded Da'eef, dated 610-700 (low confidence).
rows.detail_long: Who: The Sunan was compiled by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani (817-889); it is the third of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. What: The appointment reports establish agency by prophetic practice. Note honestly: this particular narration is graded Da'eef and dated only broadly (610-700, low confidence); the Urwah al-Bariqi report also runs in Bukhari, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah through stronger chains. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “A man from Muzainah who followed the knowledge and memorized it to me that Saeed bin al-Musayyab transmitted it. He then mentioned the rest of the tradition to the same effect.” It stands in The Office of the Judge (Kitab Al-Aqdiyah). Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 610 (dated record in the Gold Ark Library). Source: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3625.

rows.timeline_year_basis: Dated 610-622, medium confidence; shown at the earliest year
rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2311
rows.detail: Deputed to guard the sadaqa. 'Allah's Messenger deputed me to keep the Sadaqat of Ramadan' — custody agency over public alms, with the agent answerable to the principal.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Abu Hurairah. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: Abu Hurairah is appointed keeper of the zakat al-fitr stores, catches a night thief, and threatens to bring him to the Prophet — the agent enforcing on the principal's authority. Agency over other people's property, with accountability running back to the appointer. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) deputed me to keep Sadaqat (al-Fitr) of Ramadan. A comer came and started taking handfuls of the foodstuff (of the Sadaqa) (stealthily). I took hold of him and said, "By Allah, I will take you to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) ." He said, "I am needy and have many dependents, and I am in great need." I released him, and in the morning Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) asked me, "What did your prisoner do yesterday?" I said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! [...]” It stands in Representation, Authorization, Business by Proxy. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 610 (dated 610-622, medium confidence; shown at the earliest year). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2311.

rows.timeline_year_basis: Dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year
rows.display_note: Agency named explicitly — 'appointed a man as an agent in Khaybar' — and the principal corrects the agent's dealings
rows.name: Muwatta 1368

hadith_meta.narrator: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayra

rows.detail: The agent at Khaybar, supervised. The Prophet appoints an agent over Khaybar; when the agent swaps dates unequally, the principal audits and corrects the transaction.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Muwatta is the work of Malik ibn Anas (711-795), the jurist of Medina and eponym of the Maliki school. Narrator: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayra. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: 'the Messenger of Allah... appointed a man as an agent in Khaybar, and he brought him some excellent dates' — obtained, it emerges, at one-for-two. The exchange is corrected on the spot (the like-for-like rule). The principal remains responsible for HOW the agent transacts: agency does not launder a defective deal. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Yahya related to me from Malik from Abd al-Hamid ibn Suhayl ibn Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf from Said ibn al-Musayyab from Abu Said al- Khudri and from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed a man as an agent in Khaybar, and he brought him some excellent dates. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him, "Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?" He said,"No. By Allah, Messenger of Allah! [...]” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Muwatta 1368.

rows.name: Mishkat al-Masabih 1384

hadith_meta.narrator: (on) Ali; Abu Dawud transmitted it, Tirmidhi similar

rows.detail: Sacrifice performed on his behalf. Ali, sacrificing two rams: 'God's Messenger enjoined me to sacrifice on his behalf, so that is what I am doing' — delegation even in acts of worship with property.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mishkat al-Masabih is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: (on) Ali; Abu Dawud transmitted it, Tirmidhi similar. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: agency's widest reach — a ritual act involving property (the sacrifice) validly performed by a deputy on the principal's instruction, continuing after the principal's death. The doctrinal anchor for the rule that whatever a person may do himself, he may in principle appoint another to do. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “I saw Ali sacrificing two rams and asked him the meaning of it. He replied, “God’s Messenger enjoined me to sacrifice on his behalf, so that is what I am doing.” Abu Dawud transmitted it, and Tirmidhi transmitted something similar.” It stands in Prayer. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Mishkat al-Masabih 1384.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed gloss on 18:19 — the Cave companions 'send one of you with this money to the city': one purse, one deputed buyer.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas on 18:19 names the actors: the chief proposes and Yamlikha (Yamblichus) is sent 'with this money' to buy food for the group — one member deputed to transact with common funds for all. The verse classical jurists cite as the Qur'anic picture of wakala. Attribution traditional, not critical — hence 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q18:19.

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi reads 'send/appoint' (ib'athu) in 18:19 as a basis for agency.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Qurtubi (1214-1273) was an Andalusian Maliki jurist and Qur'an commentator, taught by the scholars of Cordoba; after the city fell in 1236 he moved to Egypt. His twenty-volume commentary, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qurtubi), is a general commentary written from a Maliki point of view. What: Al-Qurtubi on 18:19 reads the cave-sleepers' 'send one of you with this silver coin to the city' as delegation — one acting for the group with their money — the agency seed the fiqh manuals grow into wakala. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Wakala ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1273 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q18:19.

rows.name: Ibn Rushd
rows.detail: Ibn Rushd lists the four pillars of agency: principal, agent, subject matter, formula.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Rushd (1126-1198), known in the West as Averroes, was an Andalusian polymath and jurist of Cordoba who trained in Maliki law and served as a judge. He wrote Bidayat al-Mujtahid on the differences between the schools of law and the principles behind them; his biographer Ibn al-Abbar called him especially competent in the study of juristic disagreement. What: Bidayat's compact treatment fixes the structural anatomy of wakala the schools share. In the work itself (vol. and page 4:85; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And in it are three chapters: the first chapter: on its pillars, and it is the examination of that in which appointing an agent takes place, and of the principal. And the second: on the rulings of agency. And the third: on the principal's differing with the agent.” It also states: “And they agreed on the agency [appointing an agent] of the absent, the sick and the woman who are in charge of their own affairs. And they differed on the agency of the present, male, healthy one.” It also states: “And the condition of the agent is that he not be barred by the Law from his acting in the thing in which he was made agent.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Wakala ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1198 (year of the author's death). Source: Bidayat al-Mujtahid.

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Al-Mughni (5:71) treats agency including the fuduli — the unauthorized agent awaiting ratification.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: Ibn Qudama covers appointment, scope and the fuduli doctrine; al-Kasani's Bada'i does the same for the Hanafis. In the work itself (vol. and page 5:63; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And it is permissible by the Book and the Sunna and consensus. As for the Book, it is the saying of God, exalted is He: {the alms are only for the poor and the needy and those who work on them} [al-Tawba: 60]. So He permitted working on them, and that is by way of deputising for those entitled.” It also states: “{So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him see which of it is purest in food, and let him bring you provision from it} [al-Kahf: 19]. And this is an agency.” It also states: “[From the hadith of 'Urwa ibn al-Ja'd, cited from Abu Dawud, al-Athram and Ibn Majah:] so he gave me a dinar, and said: O 'Urwa, go to the imported goods [al-jalab] and buy us a sheep.” It also states: “[From the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, cited from Abu Dawud:] so he said: go to my agent, and take from him fifteen wasq.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Wakala ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mughni, 5:71.

rows.name: al-Quduri
rows.detail: Al-Quduri: 'Every contract, the forming of which is permitted for a human himself, it is [also] permitted for him to appoint someone else as an agent in it.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Quduri (362-428 AH) was a jurist of the Hanafi school; his Mukhtasar is the classic Hanafi primer. What: The classic Hanafi primer states the general rule of agency: whatever contract a person may make himself, he may make through an agent. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Wakala ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1037 (428 AH (death) as printed on the translation's title page; CE year by calendar conversion (428 AH = 1036-37 CE)). Source: Mukhtasar al-Quduri, chapter on Wakalah.

rows.name: Yahya ibn Sharif al-Nawawi
rows.detail: Al-Nawawi: for a valid agency 'it is necessary that the principal should have the right to do in person what he authorises his agent to do'.
rows.detail_long: Who: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (1233-1277), known as Muhyi al-Din, was a Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. His works include Minhaj al-Talibin and Riyad al-Salihin; al-Asnawi described him as the editor and refiner of the Shafi'i school. What: The standard Shafi'i manual ties the agent's power to the principal's own right to act. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Wakala ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1277 (year of the author's death). Source: Minhaj al-Talibin, Book 14 (Principal and Agent).

rows.timeline_year_basis: Adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 14, Dubai, 21-22 Rabi' I 1426 / 30 April-2 May 2005
rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 23 (Agency), adopted 2005. Investment agency becomes the workhorse of deposits, sukuk and takaful.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS23 codifies wakalah bi'l-istithmar — the fee-based investment agency now carrying more sukuk volume than any other structure. Adopted 2 May 2005 (not 2002). Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1 agency is immediate by default (effective on conclusion; conditional and future-effective forms exist); 4/1/1 general agency covers all disposal methods within the principal's interest and customary practice; 4/2/2 PAID agency falls under the ijarah rulings; 4/2/3 remuneration must be known — lump sum or a share of a specified income; 5/1/1 in procurement agency the principal bears the price and reimburses the agent's expenses; 6/1/1 the agent's deals with close relatives are permissible unless collusion against the principal's interest appears. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Wakala ladder; shown at 2005 (adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 14, Dubai, 21-22 Rabi' I 1426 / 30 April-2 May 2005). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 23 (Agency).
